content: 1. TROENTERITIS: This condition refers to inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract, specifically the stomach and intestines, which can lead to symptoms such as diarrhea, abdominal pain, and dehydration. It may require medical evaluation and management depending on severity. 2. Large Varicocele: A varicocele is an abnormal enlargement of the veins within the scrotum. When large, it can make locating the vas deferens during a vasectomy challenging or impossible. Combining varicocele repair with vasectomy in a single procedure can reduce the risk of complications. 3. Large Hydrocele: A hydrocele is the accumulation of fluid around the testicle, causing scrotal swelling. A large hydrocele can obscure the vas deferens, complicating vasectomy. Performing hydrocele repair and vasectomy simultaneously can minimize risks. 4. Filarial Elephantiasis: In cases where elephantiasis, caused by filariasis, involves the scrotum, palpation of the spermatic cord and testis may be impossible, making surgical procedures like vasectomy highly challenging. 5. Intrascrotal Mass: The presence of a mass within the scrotum may indicate an underlying pathology, such as a tumor or infection, which requires thorough evaluation before any surgical intervention. 6. Cryptorchidism: This condition, where one or both testicles fail to descend into the scrotum, can complicate vasectomy. Surgical correction of the undescended testicle may be necessary prior to sterilization. 7. Inguinal Hernia: Vasectomy can be performed concurrently with hernia repair, provided the patient is appropriately prepared and the surgical team is experienced. 8. Categories for Medical Eligibility: A (Accept): There is no medical reason to deny sterilization to individuals with this condition. C (Caution): The procedure can be performed in a routine setting but requires additional preparation and precautions. D (Delay): The procedure should be postponed until the condition is evaluated and/or corrected. Temporary contraceptive methods should be provided in the interim. S (Special): The procedure should be conducted in a specialized setting with an experienced surgical team, general anesthesia capabilities, and comprehensive medical support. Temporary contraception should be offered if referral or delay is necessary. 9. Postpartum Sterilization: <7 Days Postpartum: Sterilization can be safely performed immediately after delivery. 7 to <42 Days Postpartum: There is an increased risk of complications due to incomplete uterine involution. Pre-eclampsia/Eclampsia: These conditions increase anesthesia-related risks. Prolonged Rupture of Membranes (>24 Hours): This increases the risk of postoperative infection. Puerperal Sepsis or Fever: These conditions elevate the risk of postoperative infection. Severe Hemorrhage: Anemia from blood loss may impair the patient’s ability to tolerate further blood loss during surgery. Severe Genital Trauma: Significant blood loss and anemia may occur, complicating surgical procedures. Uterine Rupture or Perforation: These conditions may result in significant blood loss or damage to abdominal contents. 10. Post-Abortion Considerations: Sepsis or Fever: Increased risk of postoperative infection. Severe Hemorrhage: Anemia may impair the patient’s ability to tolerate further blood loss. Severe Genital Trauma: Anemia and increased pain may complicate the procedure. Uterine Perforation: Significant blood loss or damage to abdominal contents may occur. 11. Other Medical Considerations: Multiple Risk Factors for Cardiovascular Disease: Increased risk of complications from anesthesia and surgery. Ischemic Heart Disease: High risk of anesthesia and surgical complications. Cervical, Endometrial, or Ovarian Cancer: Treatment often results in sterilization. Uterine Fibroids: Large or poorly located fibroids may make it difficult to access the fallopian tubes or mobilize the uterus. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): PID increases the risk of postoperative infection or adhesions. Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs): These increase the risk of postoperative infection. Diabetes: Poorly controlled blood sugar increases the risk of hypoglycemia, ketoacidosis, and postoperative wound infections. Thyroid Disorders: These conditions increase the risk of anesthesia and surgical complications. Viral Hepatitis: High risk of complications related to anesthesia and surgery. Sickle Cell Disease: Increased risk of pulmonary, cardiac, or neurological complications, as well as wound infections. Coagulation Disorders: Increased risk of hematologic complications, such as hematoma formation, which can lead to infection. Systemic Infections or Gastroenteritis: Increased risk of postoperative infection, dehydration-related complications, and anesthesia-related risks. Fixed Uterus: Previous surgery or infection may reduce uterine mobility, complicating laparoscopy or minilaparotomy and increasing the risk of complications. Diaphragmatic Hernia: Laparoscopy may induce acute cardiorespiratory complications due to pneumoperitoneum or the Trendelenburg position. Kidney Disease: Impaired clotting, increased infection risk, and potential for hypovolemic shock. Baseline anemia, electrolyte disturbances, and altered drug metabolism/excretion may also occur. Severe Nutritional Deficiencies: Increased risk of wound infection and impaired healing. 12. Additional Comments for Male Sterilization: Diabetes: Increased risk of postoperative wound infections. Antibiotics should be administered if signs of infection appear. Local Infection: Increased risk of postoperative infection. Coagulation Disorders: Bleeding disorders increase the risk of hematoma formation, which can lead to infection. Systemic Infection or Gastroenteritis: Increased risk of postoperative infection. Large Varicocele: Locating the vas deferens may be difficult or impossible. Combining varicocele repair with vasectomy reduces complications. Large Hydrocele: Locating the vas deferens may be difficult or impossible. Combining hydrocele repair with vasectomy reduces complications. Filarial Elephantiasis: Scrotal involvement may make palpation of the spermatic cord and testis impossible. Intrascrotal Mass: May indicate underlying disease requiring evaluation. Inguinal Hernia: Vasectomy can be performed alongside hernia repair. Sickle Cell Disease: Increased risk of pulmonary, cardiac, or neurological complications, as well as wound infections.
